triage.name: Acne
triage.reason: Common dermatologic diagnosis reachable by history and skin exam, with recognizable lesion types and clear management decisions.

demographics: Affects most adolescents to some degree
Persists into adulthood in a minority, more often in women
In adults, women present for treatment more often than men

risk_factors.text: Family history of acne in a parent or sibling
Hormonal fluctuation, including the premenstrual week
Use of comedogenic cosmetics, oils, or occlusive hair products on the face
Medications such as corticosteroids, lithium, or testosterone
High glycemic-index diet or frequent dairy intake

family_history: Acne in a parent or sibling, sometimes severe enough to scar
social_history: Frequent use of heavy facial moisturizers, sunscreens, or makeup
Sports equipment or helmets rubbing the skin

chief_complaints.text: I keep getting pimples on my face
My face has bumps and blackheads that won't go away
I have breakouts on my back and chest too
The spots are leaving dark marks and scars

hpi.onset: Gradual, starting around the time of puberty or a few months after a hormonal change
hpi.duration: Weeks to years; typically intermittent and long-standing by the time of presentation
hpi.progression: Comes and goes in crops; lesions heal slowly and new ones appear, often worsening before menstrual periods
hpi.location: Face, especially the cheeks, forehead, and chin; also the back, chest, and shoulders
hpi.quality: Blackheads and whiteheads, red tender bumps, and pus-filled pimples; deeper ones feel like firm painful lumps under the skin
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for most; some have deep painful nodules and scarring
hpi.timing: Persistent with flare-ups; often worse in the week before a period
aggravating: Sweating and occlusive clothing or helmets
relieving: Gentle washing with a mild cleanser
Over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid products

associated_symptoms.text: Red tender bumps and pus-filled pimples
Dark spots left behind after lesions heal
Scarring, including pitted or raised marks
Pain or tenderness of deep lesions
Embarrassment or low mood about appearance

pertinent_negatives: Hair loss or excessive facial hair growth
New medications known to trigger acne

positives.text: Blackheads and whiteheads on the face
Red tender bumps or pus-filled pimples
Dark marks or scars where lesions healed
Lesions on the back, chest, or shoulders

argues_against: Mucosal involvement suggesting a systemic disease
Signs of an underlying endocrine disorder such as Cushing syndrome

negatives: New excess facial or body hair
argues_against: Polycystic ovary syndrome or an androgen-secreting tumor

positives.text: Feeling self-conscious or embarrassed about the skin

atypical.how_it_differs: Acne before age 8 is unusual and should prompt evaluation for early puberty or an androgen excess; lesions may be limited to the forehead and nose.
missing_classic_features: Lesions on the lower face and trunk

atypical.how_it_differs: Breakouts often flare in the first trimester and improve later; treatment options are limited, and tetracyclines and most retinoids must be avoided.

New acne after age 40, especially with sudden onset, hirsutism, or irregular periods, raises concern for an underlying endocrine cause such as polycystic ovary syndrome or an androgen-secreting tumor.
missing_classic_features: Typical distribution on the back and chest

atypical.how_it_differs: Lesions may cluster in skin folds and areas of friction, and can be mistaken for folliculitis or hidradenitis.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; skin oily in the T-zone
general.moderate: Well-appearing, may be self-conscious or avoid eye contact when discussing the skin
general.severe: Well-appearing but visibly distressed about the skin; may have scarring or dark marks
general.critical: Not applicable to acne; a toxic-appearing patient with fever and widespread tender lesions suggests another diagnosis such as disseminated infection

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face in good light, looking closely at the forehead, cheeks, and chin
findings.finding: Open comedones (blackheads) — small dark plugs at the follicular openings

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently stretch the skin around the follicles
findings.finding: Closed comedones (whiteheads) — small flesh-colored or white papules without surrounding redness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face, then the back, chest, and shoulders
findings.finding: Erythematous papules and pustules centered on hair follicles

findings.maneuver: Palpate deeper lesions on the face, back, and chest
findings.finding: Firm, tender nodules or cysts under the skin

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to expose the back, chest, and shoulders and inspect them
findings.finding: Comedones, papules, or pustules on the trunk in addition to the face

findings.maneuver: Inspect healed and healing lesions for color change
findings.finding: Brown or dark red macules where lesions have resolved

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face for textural change
Observe the shine of the facial skin and ask about oiliness
findings.finding: Seborrhea — visibly oily skin, especially the forehead and nose

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and lips
Compare involved skin with sun-protected areas such as the upper eyelids and under the chin
findings.finding: Lesions are not limited to sun-exposed skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the beard area, buttocks, and skin folds
findings.finding: No monomorphic pustules confined to hair-bearing or occluded areas

findings.maneuver: Inspect the upper lip, chin, chest, and abdomen for coarse terminal hair
Palpate the cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes

initial.why: Diagnosis is clinical: identify comedones, inflammatory papules and pustules, and their distribution on the face, back, and chest
Required before starting tetracyclines or retinoids in anyone who could be pregnant
initial.only_if: patient is a woman of childbearing potential and systemic therapy is being considered

initial.why: Screens for thyroid disease when acne is accompanied by fatigue, weight change, or other systemic symptoms
initial.only_if: features suggest an endocrine or systemic disorder

initial.why: Evaluates for cortisol excess when acne is sudden, severe, or accompanied by striae, easy bruising, or proximal weakness
Assesses for diabetes or insulin resistance when acne is accompanied by signs of hyperandrogenism or metabolic syndrome
initial.only_if: PCOS or metabolic syndrome is suspected

supporting.why: Elevated levels support hyperandrogenism when hirsutism, irregular menses, or sudden severe acne is present
supporting.only_if: signs of androgen excess are present

supporting.why: Markedly elevated levels raise concern for an adrenal androgen-secreting tumor
supporting.only_if: rapid onset of severe acne with virilization

supporting.why: Screens for nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia when androgen excess is suspected
supporting.only_if: signs of androgen excess are present

supporting.why: Evaluates ovarian morphology when PCOS is suspected

not_indicated.why: Acne does not cause blood count abnormalities; a normal result adds nothing
Not needed for a clinical skin diagnosis
Acne is not a systemic inflammatory process; CRP is normal
Histology is nonspecific and does not change management
Cutibacterium acnes is normal flora; culture does not guide therapy
Not routine; only when androgen excess is suspected
Not routine; only when an adrenal source is suspected
Not routine; only when congenital adrenal hyperplasia is suspected
Not routine; only when PCOS is suspected
Not routine; only when Cushing syndrome is suspected
Not routine; only when thyroid disease is suspected
Not routine; only when diabetes or insulin resistance is suspected
Not routine; only before starting tetracyclines or retinoids in a woman who could be pregnant

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical; no laboratory or imaging test confirms acne
Ask about irregular menses, hirsutism, and rapid onset to decide whether to test for androgen excess
Pregnancy test before isotretinoin or tetracyclines in anyone who could be pregnant
Assess for scarring and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, which push toward earlier or more aggressive therapy

differential.name: Rosacea
differential.why_considered: Facial redness with papules and pustules in an adolescent or adult

history: Flushing and blushing triggered by heat, spicy food, or alcohol
Burning or stinging rather than itching
Onset usually after age 30
exam: Papules and pustules on an erythematous background
May have eye irritation or lid margin redness

differential.name: Perioral dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Small red bumps around the mouth and nose in a young person

history: Recent use of topical corticosteroids on the face
Heavy use of facial creams or fluorinated toothpaste
Burning or tightness
exam: Monomorphic papules and pustules on an erythematous base
Narrow zone of sparing immediately around the lips

differential.name: Folliculitis
differential.why_considered: Follicle-centered pustules on the face, back, or chest

history: Recent shaving, waxing, or hot tub use
Occlusive clothing or sweating
Lesions appear in crops over days
exam: Monomorphic pustules confined to hair-bearing or occluded areas
No involvement of the forehead and chin in a typical acne pattern
labs: Gram stain and culture of pus if recurrent or severe

differential.name: Keratosis pilaris
differential.why_considered: Rough bumps on the upper arms, thighs, and sometimes the cheeks in an adolescent

history: Long-standing rough texture, often since childhood
Worse in dry winter weather
Family history of similar bumps
exam: Small keratotic follicular papules without erythema or pus

differential.name: Hidradenitis suppurativa
differential.why_considered: Painful deep nodules and draining lesions in skin folds

history: Recurrent painful boils in the axillae, groin, or under the breasts
Lesions heal with scarring and sinus tracts
Often associated with obesity or smoking
exam: Double-ended comedones, nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in intertriginous areas
imaging: Ultrasound of the affected area may show fluid collections or sinus tracts

differential.name: Steroid acne
differential.why_considered: Sudden eruption of uniform papules and pustules after starting a medication

history: Recent systemic corticosteroid, testosterone, or anabolic steroid use
Onset within weeks of starting the drug
Dose-related
exam: Monomorphic papules and pustules on the trunk, shoulders, and upper arms
May have striae or other cushingoid features with systemic steroids

differential.name: Chloracne
differential.why_considered: Comedones and cysts after exposure to halogenated aromatic compounds

history: Occupational or accidental exposure to dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls, or herbicides
Abrupt onset in an unusual age group
exam: Large comedones and cysts behind the ears, on the malar cheeks, and in the axillae
May have systemic symptoms such as neuropathy or liver toxicity
labs: Liver enzymes and serum dioxin levels if exposure is suspected

differential.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Acne with signs of androgen excess in an adolescent or adult woman
differential.trigger: Acne plus irregular or absent periods, hirsutism, or rapid onset of severe lesions

history: Irregular or absent menstrual periods
New coarse facial or body hair
Weight gain
Family history of PCOS or diabetes
exam: Hirsutism on the upper lip, chin, chest, or abdomen
Deepening of the voice or clitoromegaly suggests a tumor rather than PCOS
imaging: Pelvic ultrasound showing enlarged ovaries with multiple peripheral follicles

differential.name: Cushing syndrome
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe acne with other features of cortisol excess
differential.trigger: Acne with striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, or weight gain

history: Rapid weight gain, especially central
Easy bruising
Proximal muscle weakness
Exogenous steroid use
imaging: Pituitary MRI or adrenal CT if biochemical testing is abnormal

differential.name: Nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: Acne with hirsutism and menstrual irregularity in a young woman
differential.trigger: Androgen excess symptoms with onset near puberty or in early adulthood

history: Hirsutism
Irregular menses
Short stature or advanced bone age in childhood
Family history of similar symptoms

severity.mild: Mostly comedones with a few small papules; limited to the face; little or no scarring; minimal impact on daily life
severity.moderate: Comedones plus multiple inflammatory papules and pustules; may involve the back and chest; some postinflammatory hyperpigmentation; noticeable distress
severity.severe: Numerous inflammatory papules and pustules with deep tender nodules or cysts; widespread on face and trunk; scarring or significant hyperpigmentation; marked psychosocial impact
severity.critical: Not applicable to acne; a toxic-appearing patient with fever and widespread tender lesions suggests another diagnosis such as disseminated infection

red_flags.finding: Sudden onset of severe acne with hirsutism, deepening of the voice, or clitoromegaly
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an androgen-secreting tumor rather than typical acne; needs urgent endocrine evaluation
Suggests premature adrenarche or true precocious puberty; evaluate for an underlying endocrine disorder

red_flags.finding: Acne with wide purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, or easy bruising
red_flags.meaning: Suggests Cushing syndrome; test for cortisol excess

red_flags.finding: Fever with widespread tender pustules or nodules
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a disseminated infection or another systemic process, not acne

red_flags.finding: Mucosal erosions, blistering, or targetoid lesions
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a systemic or drug-related eruption such as erythema multiforme or Stevens-Johnson syndrome

red_flags.finding: Rapidly progressive scarring despite appropriate therapy
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an unusually aggressive course or an alternative diagnosis; consider referral and re-evaluation

complications.name: Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation
clues: Dark brown or red-brown macules at sites of healed lesions
More prominent in darker skin tones

complications.name: Atrophic or hypertrophic scarring
clues: Pitted or raised marks after deep lesions heal

complications.name: Psychosocial distress and depression
clues: Low mood or anxiety about appearance

complications.name: Gram-negative folliculitis
clues: Sudden worsening with many pustules during long-term antibiotic therapy

complications.name: Isotretinoin-associated adverse effects
clues: Teratogenicity if pregnancy occurs during or shortly after therapy

special_populations.differences: Acne before age 8 is unusual and should prompt evaluation for early puberty or androgen excess; lesions may be limited to the forehead and nose.
Breakouts often flare in the first trimester and improve later; tetracyclines and most retinoids must be avoided; topical azelaic acid and benzoyl peroxide are preferred.

New acne after age 40, especially with sudden onset, hirsutism, or irregular periods, raises concern for an underlying endocrine cause such as polycystic ovary syndrome or an androgen-secreting tumor.
Lesions may cluster in skin folds and areas of friction, and can be mistaken for folliculitis or hidradenitis suppurativa.

key_questions.question: When did the bumps start, and how have they changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset around puberty or after a hormonal change; crops of new lesions over weeks to years

key_questions.question: Where do you get them?
key_questions.looking_for: Face (cheeks, forehead, chin), and often back, chest, and shoulders

key_questions.question: What do the spots look like — blackheads, whiteheads, red bumps, pus-filled pimples, or deep painful lumps?
key_questions.looking_for: Comedones plus inflammatory papules and pustules; deep nodules suggest severe disease

key_questions.question: What makes them worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Picking or squeezing, oily or heavy skin products, sweating under helmets or occlusive clothing, stress

key_questions.question: Do the breakouts get worse before your period?
key_questions.looking_for: Premenstrual flare, which is typical of acne

key_questions.question: What have you tried so far, and how did it work?
key_questions.looking_for: Over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid, prescription topicals, oral antibiotics; partial or no response

key_questions.question: Are you using any new medicines, steroids, or hormone or bodybuilding supplements?
key_questions.looking_for: Corticosteroids, testosterone or anabolic steroids, lithium, isoniazid, phenytoin — all can trigger acne

key_questions.question: What products do you put on your face — cleansers, moisturizers, sunscreen, makeup, hair oils?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy, oily, or occlusive products that worsen acne; harsh scrubbing

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have acne, especially severe acne or scarring?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history supports the diagnosis and may predict a more persistent course

key_questions.question: Have your periods been regular? Any new coarse facial or body hair, or deepening of your voice?
key_questions.looking_for: Irregular menses or hirsutism suggests polycystic ovary syndrome or another androgen excess; voice deepening or clitoromegaly suggests a tumor

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any dark marks or scars where the spots healed?
key_questions.looking_for: Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation or scarring, which pushes toward earlier, more effective therapy

key_questions.question: How much is this affecting your mood, school, or social life?
key_questions.looking_for: Embarrassment, avoidance, low mood, or suicidal thoughts

key_questions.question: Any fever, joint pain or swelling, or new medications before the rash started?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever with widespread tender lesions, arthritis, or a drug trigger suggests another diagnosis

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status before starting tetracyclines or retinoids

reasoning_points: Gradual onset around puberty or after a hormonal change, with a chronic relapsing course
Comedones (blackheads and whiteheads) are the defining lesion, often with inflammatory papules and pustules
Distribution on the face, especially cheeks, forehead, and chin, and often the back, chest, and shoulders
No fever, mucosal involvement, or lesions limited to sun-exposed skin
No signs of androgen excess such as hirsutism, irregular menses, or voice deepening unless an endocrine cause is being considered
Diagnosis is clinical; no laboratory or imaging test confirms acne
Assess severity, scarring, and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation to guide therapy
Screen for triggers such as corticosteroids, testosterone, lithium, and comedogenic skin products

easy: Teenager with blackheads and whiteheads on the cheeks, forehead, and chin
Typical distribution on the face with some truncal involvement
No red flags and no signs of androgen excess
Clear response to over-the-counter or prescription topical therapy
medium: Adult woman with persistent breakouts along the jawline that flare before menses
Moderate inflammatory papules and pustules with postinflammatory hyperpigmentation
Acne triggered by a new medication such as prednisone or testosterone
Lesions on the back and chest with few facial lesions
hard: Sudden severe acne with hirsutism, irregular menses, or voice deepening suggesting an androgen-secreting tumor
Acne before age 8 suggesting premature adrenarche or precocious puberty
Acne with wide purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, or easy bruising suggesting Cushing syndrome
Fever with widespread tender pustules or nodules suggesting a disseminated infection rather than acne
Rapidly progressive scarring despite appropriate therapy
